Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
I try to erase the memory of the event
I think about why the event has happened to me

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For chronic physical abuse by a romantic partner, being triggered by male presence and related people is coherent, but explosion/bang sounds points toward combat, accidents, or blast-related trauma and is hard to reconcile as a core trigger here without any matching assault-context cue elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: The rest of the profile reflects fear, avoidance, hypervigilance, fragmented memory, and negative self/world appraisals. Endorsing risky behavior pulls in the opposite direction and is not supported by other selected items; it reads as a different coping/symptom pattern than the otherwise strongly avoidant-threat profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: A marked loss of connection to community and culture is not well anchored to the rest of this intimate-partner-violence profile. The other appraisals center on danger, contamination, and shattered beliefs, but nothing else suggests cultural/community rupture, making this item feel clinically disconnected rather than tightly linked to the stated trauma formulation.

vignette: Lillian, an 80‑year‑old social worker, recalls the night her former husband, whom she had loved for nearly a decade, turned violent. The memory is not a continuous narrative; it is a series of snapshots—a pounding on the door, a slamming of the front door, the feel of his hand on her cheek—each fragment flashing in her mind whenever she hears a door creak. The male presence in those images has made her view any man, even a friendly neighbor, with suspicion; her belief that the world is safe has shattered, and she feels herself physically contaminated by the abuse. Because the sight of a man immediately triggers her fear, she has begun to avoid even the dreamscape where the assault might return, hoping to erase the pain from memory. The memory of the door slamming becomes a trigger whenever any door opens, and the male presence that sparks the memory also fuels her shattered beliefs and sense of contamination. Within weeks, Lillian’s nightly routine was hijacked by hypervigilance. Each quiet housebell or sudden slam of a latch set her heart racing; she learned to scan exits the moment she entered any room, a habit that now extends to her own apartment building. These threat sensations have fueled her avoidance of dreams and the memory‑erasing practices she developed, insisting she could not allow herself to think about the abuse again. The belief that she is contaminated and that others cannot be trusted has intensified her fear of any door opening, magnifying the threat she perceives. In return, each avoidance action reinforces her sense of contamination and mistrust, and the cycle of vigilance, avoidance, and shame tightens. She is now convinced that even a polite neighbor’s smile might mask hidden violence, and that any sound of a door could herald danger. Her avoidance of any door sound has, paradoxically, amplified the door’s role as a trigger, making each creak feel like an omen. Sleep itself has become a battleground. Lillian can only fall asleep if the house is silent, but she cannot rest when a door slams or a male voice lingers in the distance. The nightmares that she tries to avoid arrive at the slightest thud, and each recall brings overwhelming grief, flooding her with the belief that the world has been irreparably broken. The grief on recall fuels her hypervigilance and the need to erase the memory, which in turn perpetuates her belief that she is unclean. The cycle of sleep disturbance, avoidance, and contamination belief leaves her with an ever‑present sense that the assault will resume, and the memory’s fragmented nature makes it impossible to put the pieces in order. Years of this relentless loop have made Lillian withdraw from her community work, leaving her clients to face challenges alone. The single life she now leads is punctuated by the constant dread of a door opening and the feeling of being unclean. She has become acutely aware that her avoidance of doors, a trigger she no longer listens to, has left her isolated in her own house. It is this unbearable combination of isolation, fear, and grief that finally pushes her to seek professional help. Lillian hopes to learn whether the weight of her contamination belief can be lifted and whether she can regain trust in the people around her without fearing the next slam of a door.
